title: Ancient Treasures

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Off the coast of Greece, near the tiny island of Antikythera, a 2,000-year-old shipwreck continues to offer up its bounty. Including life size bronze and marble statues, and a mysterious clockwork device which became known as the Antikythera Mechanism. Recently, researchers have found a partial skeleton beneath the sloping seafloor that, through DNA analysis, promises to reveal the biological details of a passenger. ‘Perhaps another mechanism or collection of sculptures wants to be freed,’ says Brendan Foley, a marine archaeologist at Lund University in Sweden and co-director of the international project. ‘Part of the excitement of this wreck,’ he says, ‘is that the possibility of discovering something stupendous is great.’

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Historians believe that in around 65 BC, when Rome ruled over the Mediterranean world, a Greek merchant vessel set out west across the Aegean Sea. ‘Measuring 165 feet in length, enormous for its time, it was loaded with luxury items probably picked up at eastern Mediterranean ports, as well as with livestock and scores of travellers,’ Foley says. ‘A storm likely cut the vessel’s trip short, smashing it against the cliffs of Antikythera. The heavily loaded ship would have sunk fast.’ Underwater, the boat skidded down a 70-degree slope before stopping 160 feet or so below the sea’s surface, unleashing debris that might have covered some cargo instantly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The ship would not be disturbed again until 1900, when a diver looking for aquatic sponges, clad in a clunky dry suit and brass helmet, saw an unattached bronze arm from a sculpture on the seabed. Subsequent dives revealed relics such as statues and personal belongings scattered across the seafloor, and Greek officials orchestrated a recovery. In 1902, fragments of the Antikythera mechanism were found while researchers were sifting through debris at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. This discovery finally brought enormous public and scientific attention to the shipwreck.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Though ancient Greek writings made reference to wondrous astronomical devices, scholars had no idea the Greeks could build something as complex as this mechanism. When whole, its tiny pieces fit together with unbelievable precision. Not until clock manufacturing in 14thcentury Europe were interlocking gears again used in a similar manner. Alexander Jones, a historian of the ancient world at New York University, US, who has studied the shipwreck and its cargo said, ‘We have nothing surviving from the Greco-Roman world in metalwork ... that is anywhere near so complex and refined.’

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It has taken decades of scholarship to reveal the mechanism’s secrets and understand the Greeks extensive knowledge of astronomy. The size of a shoebox, the device had plates on the front and back framed by a wooden case enclosing about 60 gears. The front plate had a circular dial with pointers tracking the movement of the sun, moon and five known planets across the sky during the calendar year. Tracking this is harder than it sounds from Earth’s perspective, the planets appear to move irregularly in the sky rather than freely circling. The Greeks compensated for this through ingenious engineering that periodically slowed the gears and reversed their rotation to control the orbits. The back plate was similarly impressive. It had two large dials: one displayed a Creek lunar month calendar while the other showed the twoand four-yearly cycles of athletic competitions, including the Olympics. A lever on one side of the device turned the gears to set the front and back dials in motion.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Paul Iversen, a Greek scholar at Case Western Reserve University, US, believes that craftsmen on the Greek island of Rhodes, in the eastern Mediterranean, likely created the device, and it was probably aboard the ship for delivery to a customer in northwest Greece when the storm struck. Most scholars agree that the mechanism was not a marine navigation device, and there is some consensus that it was not a science research tool. Its purpose may have been to educate and amaze small groups about the cosmos. A wealthy noble or philosopher might have brought it out as an object of interest during an evening gathering of wine and conversation. With its future secured as a museum piece, the device in a way has returned to its original function of fascinating audiences.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No similar mechanisms have been found on this wreck, but the most promising discovery has been the partial skeleton. Last year, bones from an individual’s skull, torso and limbs were recovered inches beneath the seafloor. Hannes Schroeder, a DNA specialist at the Natural History Museum of Denmark in Copenhagen, and the first person to examine the skeleton, says the bones look to be from a male between 15 and 25 years old. ‘Remarkably, the petrous bone, a thick area behind the ear known for its preservation of DNA, is intact. That, plus the cold water, provides favorable conditions for collecting usable genetic material,’ Schroeder explains. The results from DNA testing will potentially reveal geographic ancestry, inherited diseases and even finer characteristics like hair, eye and skin color. ‘We see in museums statues and personal possessions from the shipwreck, but more importantly, who were the people who owned this stuff?’ Schroeder says. ‘Here, for once, we have the chance to get really close to an individual, and nothing is closer than a person’s DNA.’
